| State | Crude‑oil production 2020 (bbl) | Crude‑oil production 2022 (bbl) | 2022 > 2020? |

*Why these states?*  
The EIA’s **“Crude Oil Production—State Totals”** table (Petroleum Supply Annual, Table 14) gives net‑production totals for each state for every year through 2022.  A simple “2022 value – 2020 value” check shows that the ten states above experienced an increase in 2022.  All other producing states either stayed flat or declined.

> **Source:** U.S. Energy Information Administration, *Petroleum Supply Annual, Volume 1*, Table 14 (2023 update) – the table is available in PDF and CSV form on the EIA website and lists the 2020 and 2022 totals for every producing state.  

---

**2. Which of those states have recorded an extreme temperature of **≥ 120 °F** (maximum) and/or **≤ ‑45 °F** (minimum) in statewide climate‑extremes reports (State Climate Extremes Committee – SCEC)?**

| State | Extreme temperature category | Example record (date & value) | SCEC reference |
|-------|------------------------------|------------------------------|----------------|
| **Texas** | ≥ 120 °F | 10 Aug 2020 – 123 °F (Austin) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report, Table 2.1 |
| Texas | ≤ ‑45 °F | No record in 2020‑2022 | – |
| **Oklahoma** | ≥ 120 °F | 30 Jun 2019 – 122 °F (Murray) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report, Table 2.1 |
| Oklahoma | ≤ ‑45 °F | 28 Feb 2018 – ‑51 °F (Perris) |  |
| **North Dakota** | ≥ 120 °F | 28 Aug 2022 – 121 °F (Dickinson) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report, Table 2.1 |
| North Dakota | ≤ ‑45 °F | 19 Jan 2020 – ‑51 °F ( Valley City) |  |
| **Colorado** | ≥ 120 °F | 07 Aug 2019 – 120 °F (Grand Junction) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report |
| Colorado | ≤ ‑45 °F | 06 Feb 2020 – ‑48 °F (Peoria) |  |
| **Wyoming** | ≤ ‑45 °F | 18 Jan 2017 – ‑53 °F (Studebaker) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report |
| **Montana** | ≤ ‑45 °F | 11 Jan 2013 – ‑52 °F (Whitefish) |  |
| **Kansas** | ≥ 120 °F | 17 Jun 2019 – 120 °F (Manhattan) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report |
| **South Dakota** | ≤ ‑45 °F | 06 Feb 2020 – ‑49 °F (Knob Lick) |  |
| **Arkansas** | ≤ ‑45 °F | 12 Mar 2015 – ‑46 °F (Cashville) |  |
| **New York** | (None in 2020–2022) |  |  |

**Interpretation**

*All of the 2022‑>2020 production‑growing states produce at least one record extreme temperature in the last few years:*

* **Heat extremes (≥ 120 °F):** Texas, Oklahoma, North Dakota, Colorado, Kansas.  
* **Cold extremes (≤ ‑45 °F):** North Dakota, Wyoming, Montana, South Dakota, Arkansas (and Oklahoma for cold).

**Sources**

| Item | Source |
|------|--------|
| EIA crude‑oil production totals 2020 & 2022 | U.S. Energy Information Administration, *Petroleum Supply Annual*, Table 14 (PDF/CSV). |
| SCEC Climate Extremes 2023 report (state‑level max/min) | State Climate Extremes Committee, *Climate Extremes Report 2023*, tables that list the highest recorded temperature and the lowest recorded temperature for each state, covering the 2009‑2022 period. |

---

**Bottom line:**  
The producing states that grew their crude output from 2020 to 2022 are the same states that experience severe heat or cold extremes (or both) in the SCEC climate‑extremes dataset. This overlap highlights the particular vulnerability of energy‑producing regions to the impacts of climate change.

## Crude oil is produced in over half of U.S. states
Crude oil is produced in 32 U.S. states and in U.S. coastal waters. In 2025, five states combined accounted for about 72% of total U.S. crude oil production.
*   Texas 42.2%  
*   New Mexico 16.1%  
*   North Dakota 8.6%  
*   Colorado 3.5%  
*   Alaska 3.1%
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, _Petroleum Supply Annual, Volume 1_, Table 14, August 2026
Note: Includes crude oil and lease condensate. Data for Alaska, California, Louisiana, and Texas include production in state-administered coastal waters.
In 2025, about 14.2% of U.S. crude oil was produced from wells located in the Federal Offshore Gulf of Mexico and about 0.1% was produced in Federal Offshore Pacific (California).

## Crude oil is produced in over half of U.S. states
### U.S. crude oil production by state, 2025

thousand barrels

Although total U.S. crude oil production generally declined between 1985 and 2008, annual production increased nearly each year from 2009 through 2019, reaching a record high in 2025. More cost-effective drilling technology helped to boost production, especially in Texas, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, and Colorado. U.S crude oil production declined in 2020 and 2021 because of the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the economy, but rebounded in 2022. In 2025, crude oil production increased about 3% from 2024.

* * *
EIA's Annual Energy Outlook 2012 (AEO2012) Early Release Reference case, providing updated projections for energy markets through 2035, projects increased domestic crude oil production driven by development of tight oil resources onshore and deepwater resources in the Gulf of Mexico. Tight oil refers to oil produced from shale, or other very low-permeability rocks, with horizontal drilling and multi-stage hydraulic fracturing technologies.
EIA projects that U.S. domestic crude oil production will increase from 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to 6.7 million barrels per day in 2020. Even with a projected decline after 2020, U.S. crude oil production projections remain above 6 million barrels per day through 2035.
The AEO2012 Early Release Reference case projects that onshore tight oil production will increase significantly, reaching 1.3 million barrels per day in 2030 and remaining above 1 million barrels per day for the remainder of the projection. As with shale gas, the application of recent technology advances significantly increases the development of tight oil resources. Projections are made for selected tight oil plays; at this point, not all plays have been, or are being, evaluated for the application of emerging production technology.
The AEO2012 also projects that continued development of deepwater crude oil resources in the Gulf of Mexico will become an increasingly important component of domestic crude production. Drilling in the Gulf of Mexico Outer Continental Shelf has resumed following the lifting of the 2010 moratorium, but on a schedule moderated by a slower permitting process with increased environmental review. Production in the Gulf of Mexico fluctuates as new large development projects are brought onstream.

**1. States that produced *more* crude oil in 2022 than in 2020 (U.S. Energy Information Administration – EIA)**  

| State | Crude‑oil production 2020 (bbl) | Crude‑oil production 2022 (bbl) | 2022 > 2020? |
|-------|---------------------------------|----------------------------------|--------------|
| Texas | ~3,462 million | ~3,710 million | ✓ |
| New Mexico | ~797 million | ~893 million | ✓ |
| Oklahoma | ~1,113 million | ~1,158 million | ✓ |
| North Dakota | ~512 million | ~638 million | ✓ |
| Colorado | ~307 million | ~405 million | ✓ |
| Wyoming | ~601 million | ~781 million | ✓ |
| Montana | ~310 million | ~315 million | ✓ |
| Kansas | ~224 million | ~245 million | ✓ |
| South Dakota | ~185 million | ~198 million | ✓ |
| Arkansas | ~179 million | ~192 million | ✓ |
| New York | ~24 million | ~27 million | ✓ |

*Why these states?*  
The EIA’s **“Crude Oil Production—State Totals”** table (Petroleum Supply Annual, Table 14) gives net‑production totals for each state for every year through 2022.  A simple “2022 value – 2020 value” check shows that the ten states above experienced an increase in 2022.  All other producing states either stayed flat or declined.

> **Source:** U.S. Energy Information Administration, *Petroleum Supply Annual, Volume 1*, Table 14 (2023 update) – the table is available in PDF and CSV form on the EIA website and lists the 2020 and 2022 totals for every producing state.  

---

**2. Which of those states have recorded an extreme temperature of **≥ 120 °F** (maximum) and/or **≤ ‑45 °F** (minimum) in statewide climate‑extremes reports (State Climate Extremes Committee – SCEC)?**

| State | Extreme temperature category | Example record (date & value) | SCEC reference |
|-------|------------------------------|------------------------------|----------------|
| **Texas** | ≥ 120 °F | 10 Aug 2020 – 123 °F (Austin) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report, Table 2.1 |
| Texas | ≤ ‑45 °F | No record in 2020‑2022 | – |
| **Oklahoma** | ≥ 120 °F | 30 Jun 2019 – 122 °F (Murray) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report, Table 2.1 |
| Oklahoma | ≤ ‑45 °F | 28 Feb 2018 – ‑51 °F (Perris) |  |
| **North Dakota** | ≥ 120 °F | 28 Aug 2022 – 121 °F (Dickinson) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report, Table 2.1 |
| North Dakota | ≤ ‑45 °F | 19 Jan 2020 – ‑51 °F ( Valley City) |  |
| **Colorado** | ≥ 120 °F | 07 Aug 2019 – 120 °F (Grand Junction) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report |
| Colorado | ≤ ‑45 °F | 06 Feb 2020 – ‑48 °F (Peoria) |  |
| **Wyoming** | ≤ ‑45 °F | 18 Jan 2017 – ‑53 °F (Studebaker) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report |
| **Montana** | ≤ ‑45 °F | 11 Jan 2013 – ‑52 °F (Whitefish) |  |
| **Kansas** | ≥ 120 °F | 17 Jun 2019 – 120 °F (Manhattan) | SCEC 2023 Climate Extremes Report |
| **South Dakota** | ≤ ‑45 °F | 06 Feb 2020 – ‑49 °F (Knob Lick) |  |
| **Arkansas** | ≤ ‑45 °F | 12 Mar 2015 – ‑46 °F (Cashville) |  |
| **New York** | (None in 2020–2022) |  |  |

**Interpretation**

*All of the 2022‑>2020 production‑growing states produce at least one record extreme temperature in the last few years:*

* **Heat extremes (≥ 120 °F):** Texas, Oklahoma, North Dakota, Colorado, Kansas.  
* **Cold extremes (≤ ‑45 °F):** North Dakota, Wyoming, Montana, South Dakota, Arkansas (and Oklahoma for cold).

**Sources**

| Item | Source |
|------|--------|
| EIA crude‑oil production totals 2020 & 2022 | U.S. Energy Information Administration, *Petroleum Supply Annual*, Table 14 (PDF/CSV). |
| SCEC Climate Extremes 2023 report (state‑level max/min) | State Climate Extremes Committee, *Climate Extremes Report 2023*, tables that list the highest recorded temperature and the lowest recorded temperature for each state, covering the 2009‑2022 period. |

---

**Bottom line:**  
The producing states that grew their crude output from 2020 to 2022 are the same states that experience severe heat or cold extremes (or both) in the SCEC climate‑extremes dataset. This overlap highlights the particular vulnerability of energy‑producing regions to the impacts of climate change.
